¶
'''wim''' (wim), ''v.'' [Cf. ''wimble''<sup>2</sup>.] To winnow grain. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''wimberry,''' ''n.'' See ''winberry.''

'''wimble'''<sup>1</sup> (wim′bl), ''n.'' [Also Sc. ''wimmle, wumil, wummle, wummel;'' < ME. *''wimbel, wymble, wymbyl,'' *''wimmel;'' cf. MD. ''wimpel,'' a wimble, = Dan. ''vimmel,'' an auger, = OSw. ''wimla'' (Molbech), an auger (not to be identified with Icel. *''veimil,'' which occurs but once, in comp. ''veimiltȳta,'' applied to a crooked person, but said by Cleasby to mean ‘wimble-stick’ (''tȳta,'' a pin?)); appar. connected with MD. ''weme,'' a wimble, ''wemelen,'' bore, this verb being appar. connected with ''wemelen,'' turn about, whirl, vibrate. The relations of these forms are uncertain. The word is certainly not allied, as Skeat makes it, to Dan. ''vindel-trappe'' = Sw. ''vindeltrappa'' = G. ''wendeltreppe,'' a spiral staircase, G. ''wendelbohrer,'' an auger, etc., words connected with the E. verb ''wind:'' see ''wind''<sup>1</sup>. From the MD. form is derived OF. ''guimbelet, gimbelet, guibelet,'' > ME. ''gymlet,'' > E. ''gimlet, gimblet:'' see ''gimlet.''] '''1†.''' A gimlet.
{{smaller block|<poem>Unto the pith a ffrenssh ''wymble'' in bore,
Threste in a braunche of roggy wilde olyve,
Threste ynne it faste.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius,'' Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 190.}}}}
{{smaller block|’Tis but like the little ''Wimble,'' to let in the greater Auger.
{{right|''Selden,'' Table-Talk, p. 26.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''mining,'' an instrument by which the rubbish is extracted from a bore-hole: a kind of

shell-auger. Some varieties of wimble, suitable for boring into soft clay, are called ''wimble-scoops.''—'''3.''' A marble-workers’ brace for drilling holes in marble. ¶ '''wimble'''1† (wim′bl), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''wymbelen'', ''wymmelen'' (= MD. ''wemelen''), bore, pierce with a wimble; from the noun.] To bore or perforate with or as with a wimble. {{smaller block|Thus we se Mars furiouse, thus Greeks euery harbory scaling,
Vp fretting the pilers, warding long ''wymbeled'' entryes. {{right|''Stanihurst'', Æneid, ii.}} And ''wimbled'' also a hole thro’ the said coffin. {{right|''Wood.''}}}} '''wimble'''2 (wim′bl), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''wimbled'', ppr. ''wimbling''. [Perhaps a corruption of ''winnow.''] To winnow. ''Withal’s Dict.'' (ed. 1608), p. 83. '''wimble'''3† (wim′bl), ''a.'' [With excrescent ''b'' (as in ''wimble''1), < Sw. ''vimmel'' (in comp. ''vimmelkantig''), whimsical, giddy, Sw. dial. ''vimmla'', be giddy or skittish (cf. MD. ''wemelen'', turn around, move about, vibrate, etc.), equiv. to ''vimmra'' (> ''vimmrig'', skittish, said of horses), freq. of ''vima'', be giddy, allied to Icel. ''vim'', giddiness (> E. ''whim'', with intrusive ''h'': see ''whim''); cf. Dan. ''vimse'', skip about, ''vims'', brisk, quick: see ''whim.''] Active; nimble. {{smaller block|He was so ''wimble'' and so wight, From bough to bough he lepped light. {{right|''Spenser'', Shep. Cal., March.}}}}
readings.c1s4:
{{smaller block|<poem>Buckle thy spirits up, put all thy wits
In ''wimble'' action, or thou art surprised.</poem>
{{right|''Marston'', Antonio and Mellida, I., iii. 2.}}}}

'''wimbrel''' (wim′brel), ''n.'' Same as ''whimbrel.''

'''wimming-dust''' (wim′ing-dust), ''n.'' Chaff. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''wimple''' (wim′pl), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wimpel, wympel, wymple, wimpil, wimpul,'' < AS. *''wimpel,'' found twice in glosses, in the spelling ''winpel,'' wimple, covering for the neck, = D. ''wimpel,'' streamer, pendant, = MLG. ''wimpel, wumpel'' = OHG. ''wimpal,'' a head-cloth, veil, MHG. G. ''wimpel,'' head-cloth, banner, pennon (> OF. ''guimple,'' F. ''guimpe,'' nun’s veil, > E. ''gimp'': see ''gimp''<sup>1</sup>), = Icel. ''vimpill'' = Sw. Dan. ''vimpel,'' pennon, pendant, streamer.] '''1.''' A covering of silk, linen, or other material laid in folds over the head and round the chin, the sides of the face, and the neck, formerly worn by women out of doors,

{{smaller block|{{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., v. 17.}}}}
'''2.''' A plait or fold. [Scotch.] —'''3†.''' A loose or fluttering piece of cloth of any sort; a pennon or flag. ''Weale.''

¶
'''wimple''' (wim′pl), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''wimpled'', ppr. ''wimpling''. [< ME. ''wimplen''; < ''wimple'', ''n.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To cover with or as with a wimple or veil; deck with a wimple; hide with a wimple.
{{smaller block|<poem>Upon an amblere esily she sat,
''Ywimpled'' wel, and on hir heed an hat
As brood as is a bokeler or a targe.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 470.}}
Fleming . . . fell asleep that night thinking of the nuns who once had slept in the same quiet cells; but neither ''wimpled'' nun nor cowled monk appeared to him in his dreams. {{right|''Longfellow'', Hyperion, iii. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' To hoodwink. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|This ''wimpled'', whining, purblind, wayward boy.
{{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., iii. 1. 181.}}}}
'''3.''' To lay in plaits or folds; draw down in folds.
{{smaller block|<poem>The same did hide
Under a vele that ''wimpled'' was full low.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. i. 4.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To resemble or suggest wimples; undulate; ripple: as, a brook that ''wimples'' onward.
{{smaller block|<poem>Amang the bonnie, winding banks,
Where Doon rins, ''wimplin’'' clear.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', Halloween.}}
<poem>She ''wimpled'' about to the pale moonbeam,
Like a feather that floats on a wind-tossed stream.</poem>
{{right|''J. R. Drake'', Culprit Fay.}}}}
'''2†.''' To lie in folds; make folds or irregular plaits.
readings.c2s3:
{{smaller block|<poem>For with a veile, that ''wimpled'' every where,
Her head and face was hid, that mote to none appeare.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VII. vii. 5.}}}}

'''wim-sheet''' (wim′shēt), ''n.'' A provincial English form of ''winnow-sheet.''

'''win'''<sup>1</sup> (win), ''v.''; pret. ''won'' (formerly also ''wan'', still provincial), pp. ''won'', ppr. ''winning.'' [< ME. ''winnen, wynnen'' (pret. ''wan, won'', pl. ''wunnen, wonnen'', pp. ''wunnen, wonnen, wunne''), < AS. ''winnan'' (pret. ''wan, won'', pp. ''wunnen''), fight, labor, contend, endure, suffer, = OS. ''winnan'' = OFries. ''winna'' = D. LG. ''winnen'' = OHG. ''giwinnan'', MHG. G. ''gewinnen'', attain by labor, win, conquer, get, = Icel. ''vinna'' = Sw. ''vinna'' = Dan. ''vinde'' (for *''vinne''), work, toil, win, = Goth. ''winnan'' (pret. ''wann'', pp. ''wunnans''), suffer, endure pain; cf. Skt. √ ''van'', get, win, also hold dear. From the same root are ult. E. ''winsome, wean, ween, wone, wont.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To acquire by labor, effort, or struggle; secure; gain.
{{smaller block|<poem>To flee I wolde full fayne,
For all this world to ''wynne''
Wolde I not so hym slayne.</poem>
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 141.}}
<poem>All you affirm, I know,
Is but to ''win'' time; therefore prepare your throats.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', Sea Voyage, v. 4.}}
<poem>We hope our cheer will ''win''
Your acceptation. ''B. Jonson'', New Inn, Prol.

Man praises man. Desert in arts or arms
''Wins'' public honor. ''Cowper'', Task, vi. 633.</poem>}}

Morals, II. 262.}}}} {{smaller|(''b'') To earn: as, to ''win'' one’s bread.}} {{smaller block|He syneweth nat that so ''wynneth'' his fode. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xxiii. 15.}}}} '''2.''' To obtain; derive; get: as, to ''win'' ore from a mine. {{smaller block|But alle thing hath tyme; The day is short, and it is passed pryme; And yet ne ''wan'' I nothing in this day. {{right|''Chaucer'', Friar’s Tale, l. 179.}}}} {{smaller block|In these two places the prisoners are engaged in quarrying and cutting stone: at Borghamn, they ''win'' stone on account of the Government; at Tjurkö, granite for private contractors. {{right|''Ribton-Turner'', Vagrants and Vagrancy, p. 508.}}}} '''3.''' To be successful or victorious in: as, to ''win'' a game or a battle. {{smaller block|Th’ report of his great acts that over Europe ran, In that most famous Field he with the Emperor ''wan''. {{right|''Drayton'', Polyolbion, iv. 314.}}}} {{smaller block|He that would ''win'' the race must guide his horse Obedient to the customs of the course. {{right|''Cowper'', Truth, l. 13.}}}} '''4.''' To accomplish by effort; achieve, effect, or execute; succeed in making or doing. {{smaller block|He coulde neuer in one hole daye with a meately good wynde ''wynne'' one myle of the course of the water. {{right|''Peter Martyr'' (tr. in Eden’s First Books on America, [ed. Arber, p. 163).}}}} {{smaller block|Thickening their ranks, and wedged in firm array, The close-compacted Britons ''win'' their way. {{right|''Addison'', The Campaign.}}}} '''5.''' To reach; attain to; arrive at, as a goal or destination; gain; get to. {{smaller block|Ye wynde inforced so moche and so streyght ayenst vs that our gouernoures sawe it was not possyble for vs to ''wynne'' nor passe Capo Maleo. {{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 63.}}}} {{smaller block|Before they could ''win'' the lodge by twenty paces, they were overtaken. {{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, ii.}}}} {{smaller block|Soon they ''won'' The top of all the topful heav’ns. {{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, v. 761.}}}} {{smaller block|And when the stony path began By which the naked peak they ''wan'', Up flew the snowy ptarmigan. {{right|''Scott'', Marmion, iii. 1.}}}} '''6†.''' To cause to attain to or arrive at; hence, to bring; convey. {{smaller block|Toax in the toile out of tene broght, ''Wan'' hym wightly away wondit full sore. {{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 6980.}}}} {{smaller block|He sall fordo thi fader syn, And vnto welth ogayne him ''win''. {{right|''Holy Rood'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 70.}}}} {{smaller block|Do that I my ship to haven ''winne''. {{right|''Chaucer'', Anelida and Arcite, l. 20.}}}} {{smaller block|“Sir,” quod she, “I knowe well youre will is not for to haue me I-loste.” “I-loste,” seide he, “nay, but I-''wonne'' to grete honour.” {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 671.}}}} '''7.''' To gain the affection, regard, esteem, compliance, favor, etc., of; move to sympathy, agreement, or consent; gain the good will of; gain over or attract, as to one’s self, one’s side, or one’s cause; in general, to attract. {{smaller block|Thy virtue ''wan'' me; with virtue preserve me. {{right|''Sir P. Sidney.''}}}} {{smaller block|She ’s beautiful, and therefore to be woo’d; She is a woman, therefore to be ''won.'' {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., v. 3. 79.}}}} {{smaller block|His face was of that doubtful kind That ''wins'' the eye, but not the mind. {{right|''Scott'', Rokeby, v. 16.}}}} '''8.''' To prevail on; induce. {{smaller block|Cannot your Grace ''win'' her to fancy him? {{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iii. 1. 67.}}}} {{smaller block|Who eas’ly being ''won'' along with them to go, They altogether put into the wat’ry plain. {{right|''Drayton'', Polyolbion, i. 430.}}}} '''9.''' In ''mining'', to sink down to (a bed of coal) by means of a shaft; prepare (a bed of coal) for working by doing the necessary preliminary dead-work: also applied to beds of ironstone and other ores. [Eng.] {{smaller|In the United States the word ''win'', as used in mining, has frequently a more general meaning; it is thus defined in the glossary of the Pennsylvania Survey: “To mine, to develop, to prepare for mining.” See ''winning''.}} {{smaller block|The shaft [at Monkwearmouth] was commenced in May, 1826; it was continued for eight and a half years before the first workable coal was reached; and it was only in April, 1846, twenty years afterwards, that the enterprise was proved successful by the ''winning'' of the “Hutton Seam.” {{right|''Jevons'', The Coal Question (2d ed.), p. 68.}}}}
